## Background

In 2023 I wrote a paper (`Final Paper.docx` / `regression.R`, both in
`/legacy` in this repository) asking whether St. Louis's Delmar Loop
Trolley raised home values in the zip codes it runs through (63130,
63112), relative to three comparison zips (63114, 63133, 63108) chosen
for similar geography and demographics. That analysis ran a separate
`lm(HomeValue ~ time + treated + did)` for each of several candidate
treatment dates (announcement in 2010, construction start in 2015,
opening in 2018) and found no statistically significant increase in home
values under any plausible treatment date -- the one specification that
*did* come back significant relied on a 20-year window and was flagged
in the paper itself as likely confounded by unrelated City/County policy
differences over that span.

This notebook revisits that question two ways:

1.  **An improved version of the original St. Louis model** -- same
    treated/comparison zips, same preferred treatment date (the
    trolley's actual opening, since that's the least ambiguous and least
    confounded of the three candidate dates), but with two changes
    standard in applied DiD work that the original didn't have: zip and
    time fixed effects instead of simple dummy variables, and standard
    errors clustered by zip (monthly home values within a zip are highly
    autocorrelated, so un-clustered OLS standard errors understate
    uncertainty).
2.  **A pooled model across all three circulators** this project now
    covers -- St. Louis, the KC Streetcar, and the Cincinnati Connector
    -- to ask the broader question the single-city design can't: do
    urban circulators raise home values *in general*, not just in one
    city.

A caveat up front: part 2's comparison zips for Kansas City and
Cincinnati have not been vetted with anything like the care the original
paper put into its St. Louis control group. That vetting is addressed
below, but it's a quick, county-level check -- not a demographic or
geographic argument on the level of the original paper. Part 2's results
should be read with that in mind.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
library(broom)
library(scales)

# The full Zillow ZHVI export (~120MB, every US zip code) is too large to
# commit to this repo. This analysis only ever touches 16 zip codes
# across three cities, so ../data/zip_data_subset.csv -- the same
# columns, just those 16 rows -- is a drop-in replacement. See
# ../data/README.md for provenance and how to regenerate it (or get the
# full national file) if you need more zips than this.
zip_data_raw <- read_csv("../data/zip_data_subset.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## Building an event-time panel

Each city's circulator opened on a different calendar date, so pooling
them requires a shared clock: *event time*, measured in months relative
to that city's own opening date, rather than calendar time.
`build_event_panel()` below takes a city's treated and comparison zips
and its opening date, reshapes the wide Zillow export into zip-month
rows, computes each row's distance from the opening date in months, and
restricts the panel to a fixed window on either side of it.

```{r build-panel-fn}
build_event_panel <- function(zip_data, treated_zips, comparison_zips, opening_date,
                               window_months = 36, city_label) {
  zips <- c(treated_zips, comparison_zips)
  date_cols <- zip_data %>%
    select(matches("^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$")) %>%
    names()
  opening_date <- as.Date(opening_date)

  zip_data %>%
    filter(RegionName %in% zips) %>%
    select(RegionName, City, CountyName, all_of(date_cols)) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = all_of(date_cols), names_to = "date_str", values_to = "HomeValue") %>%
    mutate(
      Date = as.Date(date_str),
      RegionName = as.character(RegionName),
      treated = as.integer(RegionName %in% treated_zips),
      # Whole-month distance from the opening date -- simple integer
      # arithmetic on year/month rather than lubridate period math, which
      # is more predictable across month-end dates like these.
      event_month = (year(Date) - year(opening_date)) * 12 +
        (month(Date) - month(opening_date))
    ) %>%
    filter(abs(event_month) <= window_months, !is.na(HomeValue)) %>%
    mutate(post = as.integer(event_month >= 0), city = city_label)
}
```

## Part 1: St. Louis, revisited

Treated zips (63130, 63112) and comparison zips (63114, 63133, 63108)
match my original paper exactly -- these are also the correct zips going
forward for this project; the dashboard's `stl_trend_zips` previously
had a transcription typo (63113 instead of 63114) which has been fixed
to match. Window: 36 months on either side of the November 2018 opening,
matching the paper's own preferred specification.

```{r stl-panel}
stl_treated <- c("63130", "63112")
stl_comparison <- c("63114", "63133", "63108")

stl_panel <- build_event_panel(
  zip_data_raw, stl_treated, stl_comparison,
  opening_date = "2018-11-30", window_months = 36, city_label = "St. Louis"
)
```

### Two-way fixed-effects DiD

```{r stl-model}
stl_fe <- feols(HomeValue ~ treated:post | RegionName + Date, cluster = ~RegionName, data = stl_panel)
etable(stl_fe)
```

Zip fixed effects absorb each zip's own baseline home value; date fixed
effects absorb whatever was happening to home values region-wide (or
nationally) in a given month. `treated:post` is the DiD estimate itself,
and standard errors are clustered by zip -- unlike the original `lm()`,
which had neither.

### Event study: does parallel trends actually hold?

The original paper checked parallel trends by eye ("it seems visually
that..."). This estimates a separate treated-vs-comparison gap for every
month relative to the opening (holding the month right before opening,
`event_month = -1`, as the reference), so pre-trends can be read off the
plot directly instead of inferred from a line chart.

```{r stl-event-study}
stl_es <- feols(HomeValue ~ i(event_month, treated, ref = -1) | RegionName + Date,
                 cluster = ~RegionName, data = stl_panel)
iplot(stl_es,
      main = "St. Louis: Event-Study Estimates (Loop Trolley, Nov 2018)",
      xlab = "Months relative to opening", ylab = "Treated - comparison gap (USD)")
```

If the pre-period (negative `event_month`) coefficients sit close to
zero with confidence intervals that comfortably span it, that's real
evidence for parallel trends -- not just a visual impression. If they
don't, that's worth reporting honestly rather than dropping the check.

## Part 2: Pooling all three circulators

### A quick vetting pass on the comparison zips

St. Louis's comparison zips were chosen in the original paper for
matching geography and demographics, with an explicit check that the
group balances City vs. County jurisdiction against the treated pair.
Kansas City's and Cincinnati's comparison zips, by contrast, were
originally picked for the project's dashboard trend chart -- a visual
choice, not an econometric one. A light check against each zip's
`City`/`CountyName` fields:

- **Kansas City** treated zips (64106, 64108, 64105) are all Jackson
  County. The dashboard's original comparison list included 64116, which
  is Clay County -- a different jurisdiction, exactly the kind of
  confound the original paper flagged for its own invalid long-window
  model. Swapped for **64111** (Westport / Country Club Plaza), which is
  Jackson County and, like the original paper's choice of the Central
  West End (63108) in St. Louis, is a walkable/mixed-use district that
  was *not* served by the streetcar -- the same logic, applied to Kansas
  City.
- **Cincinnati** treated zip (45202) and comparison zips (45203, 45212,
  45219, 45206) are all Hamilton County. 45212 is technically Norwood, a
  separate incorporated city within the county, not Cincinnati proper --
  a milder version of the same issue, and one I'm choosing to leave as a
  disclosed limitation rather than resolve here.

This is not the level of scrutiny the original St. Louis group received.
Treat Part 2 as a useful extension, not a replacement for Part 1.

```{r pooled-panel}
kc_treated <- c("64106", "64108", "64105")
kc_comparison <- c("64111", "64124", "64127") # 64116 (Clay County) swapped for 64111 (Jackson County)

cincy_treated <- c("45202")
cincy_comparison <- c("45203", "45212", "45219", "45206")

kc_panel <- build_event_panel(
  zip_data_raw, kc_treated, kc_comparison,
  opening_date = "2016-05-31", window_months = 36, city_label = "Kansas City"
)
cincy_panel <- build_event_panel(
  zip_data_raw, cincy_treated, cincy_comparison,
  opening_date = "2016-09-30", window_months = 36, city_label = "Cincinnati"
)

# Each city's treated/comparison zips are entirely distinct from the other
# cities' (no physical zip code appears in more than one city's panel), so
# stacking these three is simpler than the general "stacked DiD" literature
# deals with -- there's no shared pool of potential comparison units being
# reused across cohorts with different treatment timing, which is the
# problem that design was built to solve. Here it's just three independent
# local comparisons pooled into one regression for power, sharing an
# event-time clock instead of a calendar-time one.
pooled_panel <- bind_rows(stl_panel, kc_panel, cincy_panel) %>%
  mutate(
    zip_id = paste(city, RegionName, sep = "_"), # zip codes don't collide across these states, but this keeps the clustering unit unambiguous
    city = factor(city)
  )
```

### Pooled two-way fixed-effects DiD

`city^event_month` creates one fixed effect per (city, event-month)
combination -- the pooled equivalent of the date fixed effect in Part 1,
since the three cities aren't on the same calendar clock.

```{r pooled-model}
pooled_fe <- feols(HomeValue ~ treated:post | zip_id + city^event_month,
                    cluster = ~zip_id, data = pooled_panel)
etable(stl_fe, pooled_fe, headers = c("St. Louis only", "Pooled (3 cities)"))
```

### Pooled event study

```{r pooled-event-study}
pooled_es <- feols(HomeValue ~ i(event_month, treated, ref = -1) | zip_id + city^event_month,
                    cluster = ~zip_id, data = pooled_panel)
iplot(pooled_es,
      main = "Pooled Event-Study Estimates, All Three Circulators",
      xlab = "Months relative to each city's own opening date", ylab = "Treated - comparison gap (USD)")
```

The pooled event study shows a smooth, roughly linear pre-trend -- the
treated/comparison gap starts around -\$20k three years before opening
and closes to near zero right at treatment, rather than sitting flat.
That's a parallel-trends violation, not noise: the confidence intervals
in the early pre-period don't come close to including the later
pre-period estimates. Two explanations are worth distinguishing before
taking the pooled DiD coefficient at face value: (1) a genuine
anticipation effect, where nearby home values start rising as a
circulator project becomes real, well before it opens, or (2) the
comparison zips for at least one city are simply a worse match than St.
Louis's -- already on a different appreciation trajectory for reasons
that have nothing to do with the circulator. St. Louis's own event study
(above) is comparatively flat and noisy, with no equivalent monotonic
drift, which points toward (2): this pre-trend is more likely coming
from Kansas City and/or Cincinnati, whose comparison zips were picked
for the project's dashboard chart, not vetted the way St. Louis's were.

### Diagnostic: which city is driving the pre-trend?

Splitting the event study out by city (still each against its own
comparison group, no pooling) should show whether the drift is
broad-based or concentrated in the two less-vetted cities.

```{r per-city-diagnostic}
kc_es <- feols(HomeValue ~ i(event_month, treated, ref = -1) | RegionName + Date,
               cluster = ~RegionName, data = kc_panel)
iplot(kc_es, main = "Kansas City: Event-Study Estimates (Streetcar, May 2016)",
      xlab = "Months relative to opening", ylab = "Treated - comparison gap (USD)")

cincy_es <- feols(HomeValue ~ i(event_month, treated, ref = -1) | RegionName + Date,
                   cluster = ~RegionName, data = cincy_panel)
iplot(cincy_es, main = "Cincinnati: Event-Study Estimates (Connector, Sep 2016)",
      xlab = "Months relative to opening", ylab = "Treated - comparison gap (USD)")
```

**Cincinnati is driving almost all of it.** Its pre-period gap opens
around -\$60k thirty-six months before the Connector's opening and
closes smoothly to zero right at treatment -- a much larger, cleaner
version of the pooled drift. Kansas City shows a milder version of the
same pattern (roughly a \$10k pre-period close, well within its wide
confidence intervals); St. Louis, again, doesn't.

One caution on interpretation: this 36-month pre-window can't actually
adjudicate whether that drift is anticipation or an older, independent
trend. It runs from roughly September 2013 to the Connector's September
2016 opening -- which is close to when the project's funding was locked
in and construction became real, not some arbitrary earlier cutoff. That
means every point in this window already sits inside the "this is
happening" era; there's no flat, pre-momentum baseline here to compare
against. A drift that starts right when the window starts is equally
consistent with (a) anticipation of a now-credible project and (b) an
independent trend that predates the window entirely and simply continued
through it. Telling those apart would need a longer pre-period reaching
back before the project had real momentum (roughly 2009-2011): a gap
that's already wide back then points to (b); one that's flat until
momentum picks up around 2013 is more consistent with (a). That check
isn't run here, but the data to run it exists.

Priors still lean toward (b), for what it's worth: a
streetcar/circulator isn't the kind of large capital project (a new
subway line, say) that real estate markets are known to price in years
ahead of completion, and downtown/Over-the-Rhine was independently one
of Cincinnati's most visible revitalization stories of the decade
regardless of the Connector.

What the data says more cleanly, without needing to settle that
question: the post-opening coefficients show no additional departure
from wherever the pre-existing trend already had prices headed. Whatever
was moving 45202's home values before September 2016 -- neighborhood
revival, anticipation, or both -- the Connector's actual opening doesn't
appear to have added anything on top of it. Same pattern, more mildly,
in Kansas City. A combined quarter-billion dollars in construction cost
across these two projects showing no detectable marginal effect on the
home values they were partly justified by is worth sitting with on its
own, independent of how the pre-trend itself is explained.

## Discussion

A few limitations worth stating plainly rather than glossing over:

- **The pooled model fails its own parallel-trends check, and Cincinnati
  is why.** The per-city diagnostic traces the pooled pre-trend almost
  entirely to Cincinnati (a \~\$60k pre-period gap closing smoothly to
  zero right at the Connector's opening), with a milder echo in Kansas
  City; St. Louis alone is comparatively flat. That undercuts the pooled
  DiD estimate (\$9,735, not significant at conventional levels anyway)
  as evidence of a real circulator effect -- it looks much more like
  45202 (downtown/Over-the-Rhine) riding Cincinnati's broader,
  independent 2010s revitalization wave, which plausibly helped motivate
  building the Connector there in the first place rather than resulting
  from it. This is arguably the most useful finding in this document:
  not a headline effect size, but a demonstration of why checking
  parallel trends explicitly (rather than eyeballing a line chart, as
  the original paper did) matters -- a naive two-period DiD would have
  reported the \$9,735 figure with no way to know it was confounded, and
  would have had no way to catch that Cincinnati's own treated zip was
  already moving well before treatment.
- **Small N.** Even pooled, this is 6 treated zips and 10 comparison
  zips across three cities -- still a small sample for a panel
  regression, and results will be sensitive to exactly which zips are in
  each group.
- **Comparison-zip vetting is uneven, but a better comparison group
  likely wouldn't fully fix Cincinnati.** St. Louis's group has a real
  argument behind it; Kansas City's and Cincinnati's had a one-pass
  county-level check. That's worth fixing regardless, but Cincinnati's
  problem looks more like treatment-placement (the treated zip itself
  was already on a different trajectory) than a fixable comparison-zip
  mismatch alone.
- **Pooling assumes a common effect.** A heritage trolley, a modern
  streetcar, and a rebranded circulator bus are not the same
  intervention, and St. Louis/Kansas City/Cincinnati are not the same
  housing market. The pooled estimate is an average effect across three
  genuinely different cases, which is a real assumption, not a neutral
  default.
- **This is not the "stacked DiD" of Cengiz et al. (2019) in the strict
  sense** -- that design exists to handle a shared pool of control units
  reused across staggered treatment cohorts, which isn't the situation
  here since each city's units are entirely its own. Worth being precise
  about that distinction rather than borrowing the name without the
  matching problem.

## Conclusion: was it worth it?

I want to be upfront that this section is opinion, not something the
regression itself proves -- but it's the opinion this analysis leaves me
with, and I think it's worth stating plainly rather than hiding behind
hedged academic language.

None of these three projects shows a statistically detectable increase
in nearby home values, and where there's a large-looking pre/post gap
(Cincinnati, mildly Kansas City), the evidence points to a pre-existing
trend the project didn't add to, not an effect of the project itself.
That's one of the two headline justifications these projects are usually
sold on -- the other being ridership, i.e., actual transportation
utility -- and on that count the picture is mixed but not encouraging
for two of the three:

- **St. Louis's Delmar Loop Trolley** (\$51M to build) carried roughly
  12,000 riders across its entire 2024 season -- less than a single
  week's ridership on MetroBus's busiest route ([KMOV, Nov.
  2024](https://www.firstalert4.com/2024/11/11/loop-trolley-ends-season-operating-within-budget-with-44-percent-increase-ridership/);
  [MetroBus systemwide
  ridership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroBus_(St._Louis))).
- **The Cincinnati Bell Connector** (\$148M) hit a record \~1.2 million
  riders in 2024 (\~3,300/day averaged across the year), but SORTA's
  single busiest bus route alone carries roughly 9,700 weekday boardings
  -- more than double the streetcar's daily average across its whole
  loop ([Connector
  ridership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connector_(Cincinnati))).
- **The KC Streetcar** (\$102M for the original starter line) actually
  complicates this story: 2025 ridership (\~2.16 million/year,
  \~5,900/day) now exceeds a comparable busy RideKC bus route on a
  per-day basis ([KC Streetcar
  ridership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KC_Streetcar)). By raw
  ridership, it's a genuine transit success relative to St. Louis and
  Cincinnati -- but matching a bus route's ridership at roughly
  \$46M/mile (and a since-built extension north of \$100M/mile) only
  pencils out as a good use of money if there's something *besides*
  moving the same number of people a bus already moves -- the usual
  pitch being exactly the property-value uplift this analysis is built
  to detect. That uplift isn't there for KC either. Good ridership
  without a value externality just means you paid a rail premium for
  what a bus route already does. A sharper cut on the same point, using
  the metric that actually measures reliance rather than total trips:
  2016-2020 Census commuting data put bus at roughly 8,500 primary
  work-commuters in the KC metro against about 250 for the streetcar --
  a 34-to-1 gap -- while KCATA's entire annual operating budget
  (\$57.6M) ran at about a fifth of the \$351M streetcar extension that
  broke ground the same year. I wrote about this specific tension for
  the Show-Me Institute in 2022, well before this analysis existed:
  ["As Kansas City's Streetcar Expands, Its Buses
  Suffer"](https://showmeinstitute.org/article/transportation/as-kansas-citys-streetcar-expands-its-buses-suffer/).
  It's a good sign, not a coincidence, that a rigorous causal analysis
  four years later lands in the same place a much simpler
  descriptive comparison did.

So the ridership case for calling these "real transit" rather than a
civic amenity is weak for St. Louis and Cincinnati, mixed-to-positive
for Kansas City. But the property-value case -- tested directly here --
comes back null for all three, including Kansas City. If a marginal
transit dollar is supposed to either move people or move property
values, and a combined several hundred million dollars across these
three projects didn't clearly do either relative to just running more
buses on routes that already carry many times the ridership, that's a
real strike against how that money was spent, not just an academic null
result to shrug off. I'd rather see that dollar go toward frequency and
coverage on the bus network already doing the actual work of moving
people in these cities.

(Ridership and cost figures above are from Wikipedia's sourced ridership
tables and local news coverage, current as of late 2025/2025-season
reporting where available; route-level bus comparisons in particular are
order-of-magnitude estimates from secondary sources and are worth a
final check against each transit agency's own published ridership
reports before this goes out publicly. The KC commute-mode-share figures
are 2016-2020 American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B08006,
as cited in the linked 2022 Show-Me Institute piece.)

## Note on results

This notebook has been rendered and reviewed -- see the Conclusion above
for the headline takeaway, and the per-city diagnostic in Part 2 for why
the pooled coefficient shouldn't be read at face value. If the
underlying zip lists, windows, or opening dates change later, re-check
the event-study plots for new pre-trend issues before trusting any point
estimate that comes out of a re-render; a clean-looking coefficient
table next to a sloped pre-trend plot is exactly the failure mode this
document was built to catch.
